The United Nations Children’s Fund has raised concerns over the growing education gap in Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara states, revealing that efforts to return hundreds of thousands of out-of-school children to classrooms have reached only a fraction of those identified. The organisation said of the approximately 624,000 children identified as out of school across the three states, only 68,000 had so far been reached through UNICEF-supported re-enrolment interventions. Speaking at a media briefing to commemorate the 2026 World Children’s Day in Sokoto on Friday, the Chief of UNICEF Sokoto Field Office, Dr Michael Juma, said the figures highlighted the need for stronger government commitment, sustained investment and community mobilisation to tackle barriers preventing children from accessing education. Juma identified journalists as important partners in advancing children’s rights, urging media organisations to intensify advocacy, promote accountability and draw attention to challenges affecting children’s welfare. “Journalists are important duty-bearers in advancing children’s rights. We need the media to provide balanced coverage that highlights development achievements while also drawing attention to the gaps that still exist,” he said. According to him, approximately 98,000 children across the three states had also benefited from the Teaching at the Right Level approach, designed to improve foundational literacy and numeracy. On healthcare, Juma disclosed that approximately 7.8 million children were reached through measles-rubella vaccination campaigns across the three states, while more than five million children received polio vaccines during the last concluded campaign. He added that in Kebbi State, where malaria vaccination had been introduced, about 148,000 children had received the first dose, while 130,000 had received the second dose. The UNICEF chief also highlighted government contributions towards tackling malnutrition, noting that Sokoto and Zamfara states committed approximately N100m and N500m respectively for the procurement of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food for children suffering from severe acute malnutrition. 2027: Obi promises 10,000 primary healthcare centres, 40,000 classrooms 624,000 children out of school in Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara – UNICEF UNICEF urges FG to involve youths in decisions, fund child nutrition He further acknowledged the Kebbi State Government’s contribution of about N540m towards free medical care for children. On access to healthcare through social health insurance initiatives, Juma said UNICEF-supported interventions had recorded approximately 86,000 beneficiaries in Zamfara, 18,000 in Sokoto and 10,000 in Kebbi. He also said UNICEF had supported the development of child protection legislation, Family Court Rules and social protection policies to strengthen the protection and rehabilitation of vulnerable children, including those in conflict with the law. Despite the interventions, Juma acknowledged that reaching the remaining out-of-school children remained a major challenge, stressing the need for stronger collaboration among government institutions, development partners and communities. Addressing concerns over declining global funding, he explained that the challenge was not peculiar to Nigeria, adding that UNICEF was expanding its resource mobilisation efforts to sustain support for state governments and essential services. He, however, assured that education programmes across Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara had not been affected by the funding decline experienced earlier in the year. On reaching children in hard-to-access communities affected by insecurity, he explained that UNICEF worked with government structures through field facilitators and third-party monitoring arrangements to ensure vulnerable children and women were not excluded from essential interventions. Juma called for stronger collaboration among government institutions, development partners, civil society organisations, traditional and religious leaders and community structures to improve service delivery. He urged journalists to use their platforms to enlighten communities, encourage demand for essential services and hold relevant authorities accountable for commitments made towards children’s welfare. “We want the media to help enlighten communities, generate demand for essential services, highlight emerging challenges and hold stakeholders accountable for the commitments they have made towards children,” he said.
